Global magnetic confinement for the 1.5D Vlasov-Maxwell systemThanks: Research of T.T. Nguyen and W.A. Strauss was supported in part by the NSF under grants DMS-1405728 and DMS-1007960, respectively. Research of T.V. Nguyen was partially supported by the Simons Foundation under grant # 318995.

Toan T. Nguyen Address: Department of Mathematics, Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA 16802, USA Email address: nguyen@math.psu.edu , Truyen V. Nguyen Address: Department of Mathematics, The University of Akron, Akron, OH 44325, USA Email address: tnguyen@uakron.edu and Walter A. Strauss Address: Department of Mathematics and Lefschetz Center for Dynamical Systems, Brown University, Providence, RI 02912, USA. Email address: wstrauss@math.brown.edu.
Abstract.

We establish the global-in-time existence and uniqueness of classical solutions to the “one and one-half” dimensional relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell systems in a bounded interval, subject to an external magnetic field which is infinitely large at the spatial boundary. We prove that the large external magnetic field confines the particles to a compact set away from the boundary. This excludes the known singularities that typically occur due to particles that repeatedly bounce off the boundary. In addition to the confinement, we follow the techniques introduced by Glassey and Schaeffer, who studied the Cauchy problem without boundaries.

1. Introduction

Using external magnetic fields to confine plasmas has been one of major goals of fusion energy research. It is one of the most promising mechanisms for producing safe new sources of fusion energy. Scientists are particularly interested in designing stable devices to induce confinement (e.g., [Ga, Wh]). In this paper we establish global-in-time magnetic confinement of a collisionless plasma, albeit under an assumption of low dimension.

Specifically, we consider the relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell (RVM) system, subject to an external magnetic field BextB_{\text{ext}} in a bounded interval Ω=(0,1)\Omega=(0,1). We assume a single species of particles with a nonnegative distribution function f⁡(t,x,v)f(t,x,v), where t≥0t\geq 0, x∈Ωx\in\Omega and v∈ℝ2v\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}. In this 1⁤121\frac{1}{2} dimensional model the Vlasov equation is

(1.1) ∂tf+v^1​∂xf+(E1+v^2​Bˇ)​∂v1f+(E2−v^1​Bˇ)​∂v2f=0,\partial_{t}f+\hat{v}_{1}\partial_{x}f+(E_{1}+\hat{v}_{2}\check{B})\partial_{v_{1}}f+(E_{2}-\hat{v}_{1}\check{B})\partial_{v_{2}}f=0,

where Bˇ=B⁡(t,x)+Bext​(x)\check{B}=B(t,x)+B_{\text{ext}}(x) with Bext​(x)B_{\text{ext}}(x) is a stationary external magnetic field that becomes infinitely large on the boundary. The internal electric and magnetic field with components E1​(t,x),E_{1}(t,x), E2​(t,x),B⁡(t,x)E_{2}(t,x),B(t,x) satisfies the 1⁤121\frac{1}{2}D Maxwell equations

(1.2) {∂tE1=−j1;∂xE1=ρ;∂tE2=−∂xB−j2,∂tB=−∂xE2.\left\{\begin{array}[]{rl}\partial_{t}E_{1}&=-j_{1};\quad\partial_{x}E_{1}=\rho;\\ \partial_{t}E_{2}&=-\partial_{x}B-j_{2},\\ \partial_{t}B&=-\partial_{x}E_{2}.\end{array}\right.

For mathematical simplicity all the physical constants have been normalized. In this relativistic case, the velocity is v^=(v^1,v^2)=v/1+|v|2\hat{v}=(\hat{v}_{1},\hat{v}_{2})={v}/{\sqrt{1+|v|^{2}}}. The charge density ρ\rho and the current density j=(j1,j2)j=(j_{1},j_{2}) are

ρ⁡(t,x):=∫ℝ2f⁡(t,x,v)​𝑑vandj⁡(t,x):=∫ℝ2v^​f​(t,x,v)​𝑑v.\displaystyle\rho(t,x):=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{f(t,x,v)\,dv}\quad\mbox{and}\quad j(t,x):=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{\hat{v}f(t,x,v)\,dv}.

We impose the standard initial conditions for the distribution function and the field, namely,

(1.3) f⁡(0,x,v)=f0​(x,v)≥0,E2​(0,x)=E20​(x),B⁡(0,x)=B0​(x),f(0,x,v)=f^{0}(x,v)\geq 0,\quad E_{2}(0,x)=E_{2}^{0}(x),\quad B(0,x)=B^{0}(x),

while the initial value for E1E_{1} is already determined by means of the identity ∂xE1=ρ\partial_{x}E_{1}=\rho and the specification

(1.4) E1​(0,0)=λE_{1}(0,0)=\lambda

for a given constant λ∈ℝ\lambda\in{\mathbb{R}}.

The novelty of this paper lies in the boundary conditions. We assume

(1.5) E2(t,x)|∂Ω=E2b(t,x),B(t,x)|∂Ω=Bb(t,x),E_{2}(t,x)_{|_{\partial\Omega}}=E_{2}^{b}(t,x),\qquad B(t,x)_{|_{\partial\Omega}}=B^{b}(t,x),

where E2b​(t,⋅)E_{2}^{b}(t,\cdot), Bb​(t,⋅)B^{b}(t,\cdot) are given functions defined on the boundary. In the sequel we will show that no particle trajectory can reach the boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega if it begins away from it. Because the particle density f⁡(t,x,v)f(t,x,v) is constant along each particle trajectory, no boundary condition is needed for f⁡(t,x,v)f(t,x,v), assuming that its initial support does not meet the boundary.

Throughout the paper we take Bext=∂xψext​(x)B_{\text{ext}}=\partial_{x}\psi_{\text{ext}}(x), in which the potential function ψext​(x)\psi_{\text{ext}}(x) is assumed to satisfy:

(1.6) ψext∈C2​(Ω)and|ψext​(x)|≥c0dist​(x,∂Ω)γ−1c0∀x∈Ω\psi_{\text{ext}}\in C^{2}(\Omega)\quad\mbox{and}\quad|\psi_{\text{ext}}(x)|\geq\frac{c_{0}}{\text{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^{\gamma}}-\frac{1}{c_{0}}\quad\quad\forall~x\in\Omega

for some constants γ>0\gamma>0 and c0>0c_{0}>0. In particular, ψext​(x)=∞\psi_{\text{ext}}(x)=\infty on the boundary!

We are interested in the well-posedness of the initial-boundary value problem (1.1)–(1.5). In what follows, C1​(U)C^{1}(U) denotes the standard C1C^{1} function space, and C01​(U)C^{1}_{0}(U) consists of functions in C1​(U)C^{1}(U) that have compact support in UU. In particular, f∈C01​([0,T]×Ω×ℝ2)f\in C^{1}_{0}([0,T]\times\Omega\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}) means that ff has compact support in the (x,v)(x,v)-variable, but has no restriction in the tt-variable. We now state our main result.

Theorem 1.1 (Global well-posedness).

Assume that f0∈C01​(Ω×ℝ2)f^{0}\in C^{1}_{0}(\Omega\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}) is nonnegative, λ∈ℝ\lambda\in{\mathbb{R}} and E20,B0,E2b,Bb∈C1E_{2}^{0},\ B^{0},\ E_{2}^{b},\ B^{b}\in C^{1}. Assume also that the external magnetic field Bext=∂xψextB_{\text{ext}}=\partial_{x}\psi_{\text{ext}} satisfies (1.6). Then the problem (1.1)–(1.5) has a unique global-in-time C1C^{1} solution (f,E1,E2,B)(f,E_{1},E_{2},B). Moreover, ff is nonnegative and f∈C01​([0,T]×Ω×ℝ2)f\in C^{1}_{0}([0,T]\times\Omega\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2})\, for any T>0T>0.

Let us mention a few previous results on the global Cauchy problem for the Vlasov–Maxwell system. It is well known that global weak solutions exist in the whole three-dimensional space ([DiL]), even in the presence of boundaries ([Gu1, M]). However, it is a famous open problem as to whether such solutions are unique or regular. Concerning classical (smooth) solutions, the authors in [GStr] established the global theory for RVM systems in the whole three-dimensional space under an assumption on the momentum support of the density. Alternative proofs have been given in [BGP, KS]. Subsequently, there was a series of papers [GSc, GSc2, GSc2.5] where the (unconditional) well-posedness and regularity of solutions were established for the 1⁤121\frac{1}{2}, 22, and 2⁤122\frac{1}{2} dimensional RVM system. The present paper is motivated by [GSc], our novelty being the presence of a boundary.

There have been just a few mathematical studies of the magnetic confinement problem (e.g., [HK, CCM1, CCM2]). All these papers are concerned with a plasma with no internal magnetic field but confined by an external magnetic field. In [HK] further assumptions are introduced that reduce the problem to a system for the macroscopic density and electric field. In [CCM1, CCM2] Vlasov-Poisson systems with bounded and unbounded charges are considered and an existence-uniqueness theorem is proved.

When confining a plasma modeled by RVM to a spatial domain, singularities are typically created at the boundary and they propagate inside the domain. This is true even for Vlasov-Poisson (VP) systems (i.e., without magnetic fields); see, e.g., [Gu2]. Furthermore, some particles repeatedly bounce off the boundary, making it extremely difficult to analyze their trajectories. To the best of our knowledge, there is no global theory of classical C1C^{1} solutions to the RVM systems in domains with boundaries, even for the simplest RVM model, the 1⁤121\frac{1}{2} dimensional system (1.1)–(1.2) without an external magnetic field.

However, in our problem with a very intense external magnetic field at the boundary, singularities can be avoided because the particles that come near the boundary are drifted back into the plasma domain. Rigorous details of the confinement are provided in Section 3. The proof of our main theorem then follows along the lines of [GSc].

The proof of Theorem 1.1 relies on uniform a priori estimates. Let us consider a C1C^{1} solution (f,E1,E2,B)(f,E_{1},E_{2},B) of the RVM equations (1.1)–(1.5) on a finite time interval [0,T][0,T] so that f⁡(t,x,v)=0f(t,x,v)=0 at the boundary x=0,1x=0,1. We shall derive L∞L^{\infty} estimates for the fields of such solution. For convenience, we rewrite (1.1) as

(2.7) ∂tf+v^1​∂xf+K⋅∇vf=0\partial_{t}f+\hat{v}_{1}\partial_{x}f+K\cdot\nabla_{v}f=0

with K:=E+(v^2,−v^1)​BˇK:=E+(\hat{v}_{2},-\hat{v}_{1})\check{B}. Hereafter we use EE to denote the vector (E1,E2)(E_{1},E_{2}).

(2.9) ∫Ωρ⁡(t,x)​𝑑x=∫Ωρ⁡(0,x)​𝑑x=‖f0‖L1​(Ω×ℝ2)=:‖f0‖1.\int_{\Omega}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_{\Omega}\rho(0,x)\,dx=\|f^{0}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2})}=:\|f^{0}\|_{1}.

We conclude from (2.10) and (2.9) that

(2.11) ‖E1‖L∞​([0,T]×Ω)≤‖f0‖1+λ.\|E_{1}\|_{L^{\infty}([0,T]\times\Omega)}\leq\|f^{0}\|_{1}+\lambda.

Lemma 2.2 (Key cone estimate).

Proof.

Let

Remark 3.2.

The condition ∂tB=−∂xE2\partial_{t}B=-\partial_{x}E_{2} is not necessary for the validity of Lemma 3.1. Indeed, an inspection of the above proof reveals that it is enough to assume the quantity ∂tB+∂xE2\partial_{t}B+\partial_{x}E_{2} to be bounded.

Lemma 3.1 shows that the particles never reach ∂Ω\partial\Omega in a finite time. As a consequence, we obtain the following corollary.

Corollary 3.3.

Let EE and BB be as in Lemma 3.1. Then for any (t,x,v)∈(0,T]×Ω×ℝ2(t,x,v)\in(0,T]\times\Omega\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}, the characteristic system (3.21) admits a unique C1C^{1} solution (X⁡(s),V⁡(s))(X(s),V(s)) in [0,T][0,T] with X⁡(s)∈ΩX(s)\in\Omega  for every s∈[0,T]s\in[0,T].

Since ‖E‖L∞​([0,T]×Ω)≤C0:=‖f0‖1+λ+C1\|E\|_{L^{\infty}([0,T]\times\Omega)}\leq C_{0}:=\|f^{0}\|_{1}+\lambda+C_{1} by Corollary 2.4, we have as in the proof of Lemma 3.1 that

Lemma 4.2.

Assume in addition that f∈C2​([0,T]×Ω×ℝ2)f\in C^{2}([0,T]\times\Omega\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}). There exists a constant CT>0C_{T}>0 depending only on k0,T,λk_{0},\,T,\,\lambda, ‖Bext‖C1​([θ1,1−θ1])\|B_{\text{ext}}\|_{C^{1}([\theta_{1},1-\theta_{1}])}, the C1C^{1} norms of f0,E20,B0f^{0},\,E_{2}^{0},\,B^{0}, and the C1C^{1} norms of E2b​(⋅,x),Bb​(⋅,x)E_{2}^{b}(\cdot,x),\,B^{b}(\cdot,x) on [0,T][0,T] (x=0, 1x=0,\,1) such that

‖f‖C1​([0,T]×Ω¯×ℝ2)+‖E‖C1​([0,T]×Ω¯)+‖B‖C1​([0,T]×Ω¯)≤CT.\|f\|_{C^{1}([0,T]\times\overline{\Omega}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2})}+\|E\|_{C^{1}([0,T]\times\overline{\Omega})}+\|B\|_{C^{1}([0,T]\times\overline{\Omega})}\leq C_{T}.

We begin with the fields EE and BB. Since ∂tE1=−j1\partial_{t}E_{1}=-j_{1} and ∂xE1=ρ\partial_{x}E_{1}=\rho, we get from Corollary 3.5 that ‖∇E1‖L∞​([0,T]×Ω¯)≤2​‖f0‖∞​(k0+C2​T)2\|\nabla E_{1}\|_{L^{\infty}([0,T]\times\overline{\Omega})}\leq 2\|f^{0}\|_{\infty}(k_{0}+C_{2}T)^{2}. These together with Corollary 2.4 give ‖E‖C1​([0,T]×Ω¯)≤CT\|E\|_{C^{1}([0,T]\times\overline{\Omega})}\leq C_{T}. On the other hand, the C1C^{1} estimate for BB is a consequence of the fact ∂tB=−∂xE2\partial_{t}B=-\partial_{x}E_{2}, Lemma 4.1 and Corollary 3.5.

Next we estimate the derivatives of ff. By differentiating the Vlasov equation (2.7) with respect to xx and vv respectively, one has

‖∂xf⁡(t)‖L∞​([θ0,1−θ0]×B¯R)≤‖∂xf0‖∞+∫0t‖∂xK‖L∞​([0,T]×[θ1,1−θ1]×ℝ2)​‖∇vf​(s)‖∞​𝑑s\displaystyle\|\partial_{x}f(t)\|_{L^{\infty}([\theta_{0},1-\theta_{0}]\times\bar{B}_{R})}\leq\|\partial_{x}f^{0}\|_{\infty}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\partial_{x}K\|_{L^{\infty}([0,T]\times[\theta_{1},1-\theta_{1}]\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2})}\|\nabla_{v}f(s)\|_{\infty}\,ds

and

‖∇vf​(t)‖L∞​([θ0,1−θ0]×B¯R)\displaystyle\|\nabla_{v}f(t)\|_{L^{\infty}([\theta_{0},1-\theta_{0}]\times\bar{B}_{R})}
≤‖∇vf0‖∞+∫0t[‖∇vv^1‖∞​‖∂xf⁡(s)‖∞+‖∇v⋅K‖L∞​([0,T]×[θ1,1−θ1]×ℝ2)​‖∇vf​(s)‖∞]​𝑑s.\displaystyle\leq\|\nabla_{v}f^{0}\|_{\infty}+\int_{0}^{t}\Big[\|\nabla_{v}\hat{v}_{1}\|_{\infty}\|\partial_{x}f(s)\|_{\infty}+\|\nabla_{v}\cdot K\|_{L^{\infty}([0,T]\times[\theta_{1},1-\theta_{1}]\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2})}\|\nabla_{v}f(s)\|_{\infty}\Big]\,ds.

5. Proof of the main result

Suppose that (f~,E~,B~)(\tilde{f},\tilde{E},\tilde{B}) and (f∗,E∗,B∗)(f^{*},E^{*},B^{*}) are two global C1C^{1} solutions to the problem (1.1)–(1.5). Define

Proof of Theorem 1.1, the existence part.

Given our results obtained in Sections 2–4, the proof of the existence of a global C1C^{1} solution follows via a the standard iteration scheme. This procedure is presented in [GSc] and [G, Chapter 5], and we shall only indicate the main points. By a standard density argument, one can assume in addition that ψext∈C3​(Ω)\psi_{\text{ext}}\in C^{3}(\Omega), f0∈C02​(Ω×ℝ2)f^{0}\in C^{2}_{0}(\Omega\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}), E20,B0∈C2​(Ω¯)E_{2}^{0},\,B^{0}\in C^{2}(\overline{\Omega}) and E2b​(⋅,x),Bb​(⋅,x)∈C2​([0,∞))E_{2}^{b}(\cdot,x),B^{b}(\cdot,x)\in C^{2}([0,\infty)) at each x=0,1x=0,1.

Let T>0T>0 be arbitrary. We recursively define a sequence of solutions {(fn,En,Bn)}\{(f^{n},E^{n},B^{n})\} to the corresponding linear equations and show that it converges to a solution of the nonlinear problem (1.1)–(1.5). For the initial step (n=0n=0), we take f0​(t,x,v):=f0​(x,v)f^{0}(t,x,v):=f^{0}(x,v), and

E0​(t,x):=∫0x∫ℝ2f0​(y,v)​𝑑v​𝑑y+λ,E20​(t,x):=E20​(x),B0​(t,x):=B0​(x).E^{0}(t,x):=\int_{0}^{x}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}f^{0}(y,v)\,dvdy+\lambda,\quad E^{0}_{2}(t,x):=E^{0}_{2}(x),\quad B^{0}(t,x):=B^{0}(x).

For n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, assume that E1n−1,E2n−1,Bn−1∈C2​([0,T]×Ω¯)E^{n-1}_{1},\,E^{n-1}_{2},\,B^{n-1}\in C^{2}([0,T]\times\overline{\Omega}) are already given. Let Kn−1:=En−1+(v^2,−v^1)​(Bn−1+Bext)K^{n-1}:=E^{n-1}+(\hat{v}_{2},-\hat{v}_{1})\big(B^{n-1}+B_{\text{ext}}\big) and denote (Xn​(s),Vn​(s))\big(X^{n}(s),V^{n}(s)\big) the solution of the characteristics system associated to a point (t,x,v)∈[0,T]×Ω×ℝ2(t,x,v)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}. That is,

(5.46) {d​Xnd​s=V^1n​(s),d​Vnd​s=Kn−1​(s,Xn,Vn),Xn(t;t,x,v)=x,Vn(t;t,x,v)=v.\left\{\begin{array}[]{rl}&\frac{dX^{n}}{ds}=\hat{V}^{n}_{1}(s),\\ &\frac{dV^{n}}{ds}=K^{n-1}(s,X^{n},V^{n}),\\ &X^{n}(t;t,x,v)=x,\quad V^{n}(t;t,x,v)=v.\end{array}\right.

Since Kn−1∈C2​([0,T]×Ω×ℝ2)K^{n-1}\in C^{2}([0,T]\times\Omega\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}), we know that (Xn,Vn)∈C2​([0,T],ℝ3)(X^{n},V^{n})\in C^{2}([0,T];{\mathbb{R}}^{3}). Then fn∈C2​([0,T]×Ω×ℝ2)f^{n}\in C^{2}([0,T]\times\Omega\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}) and it satisfies the initial value problem

and E2n,BnE^{n}_{2},\,B^{n} as the solution of

Moreover, by following the arguments in [G, Section 5.8] we see that {(fn,E1n,E2n,Bn)}\{(f^{n},E^{n}_{1},E^{n}_{2},B^{n})\} is a Cauchy sequence in the C1C^{1} norm. Consequently, there exist f∈C1​([0,T]×Ω¯×ℝ2)f\in C^{1}([0,T]\times\overline{\Omega}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}) and E1,E2,B∈C1​([0,T]×Ω¯)E_{1},E_{2},B\in C^{1}([0,T]\times\overline{\Omega}) such that fn→ff^{n}\to f, E1n→E1E^{n}_{1}\to E_{1}, E2n→E2E^{n}_{2}\to E_{2}, Bn→BB^{n}\to B uniformly for t∈[0,T],x∈Ω¯,v∈ℝ2t\in[0,T],\,x\in\overline{\Omega},\,v\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}, together with all their first derivatives. In particular, the function f,E2f,E_{2} and BB satisfy the initial and boundary conditions (1.3)–(1.5). Note also that f∈C01​([0,T]×Ω×ℝ2)f\in C^{1}_{0}([0,T]\times\Omega\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}) since the (x,v)(x,v)- support of fnf^{n} is bounded uniformly in nn by Lemma 3.4.

Passage to the limit in (5.47) yields the Vlasov equation. On the other hand, passage to the limit in (5.48) and (5.49) yields

{E1​(t,x)=∫0xρ⁡(t,y)​dy+λ,∂tE2=−∂xB−j2,∂tB=−∂xE2.\left\{\begin{array}[]{rl}&E_{1}(t,x)=\int_{0}^{x}\rho(t,y)\,dy+\lambda,\\ &\partial_{t}E_{2}=-\partial_{x}B-j_{2},\quad\partial_{t}B=-\partial_{x}E_{2}.\end{array}\right.

Thus (f,E1,E2,B)(f,E_{1},E_{2},B) is a C1C^{1} solution to the problem (1.1)–(1.5) in the time interval [0,T][0,T]. Due to the arbitrariness of TT and the uniqueness of C1C^{1} solutions presented earlier, we infer that the problem (1.1)–(1.5) admits a global classical solution (f,E,B)(f,E,B) with f∈C1​([0,∞)×Ω¯×ℝ2)f\in C^{1}([0,\infty)\times\overline{\Omega}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}) and E,B∈C1​([0,∞)×Ω¯)E,B\in C^{1}([0,\infty)\times\overline{\Omega}). Moreover, f∈C01​([0,T]×Ω×ℝ2)f\in C^{1}_{0}([0,T]\times\Omega\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}) for every T>0T>0.

We finally note that the non-negativity of the solution ff is inherited from that of f0f^{0} as ff is constant along the characteristics. ∎
